title: A smooth connected affine group without a nontrivial torus is unipotent
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be a smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] connected [def-weil-connected-scheme] affine group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$. Closed subgroup schemes are as in [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. A torus subgroup means a closed subgroup isomorphic over $k$ to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for an integer $r\geq0$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Assume that every torus subgroup of $G$ is trivial. Then $G$ is unipotent in the following explicit sense: there exist an integer $m\geq1$ and a homomorphism $\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_{m,k}$ [def-sc-general-linear-group] which is a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion] and such that, for every $g\in G(k)$, the matrix $\rho(g)-I_m$ is nilpotent, that is, $(\rho(g)-I_m)^N=0$ for some integer $N\geq1$.

source.place: Proposition 16.60, printed p.346 (PDF p.358); faithful-representation and geometric-unipotence formulation from Theorem 4.9 and Corollary 4.10, printed p.87, and Corollaries 14.6 and 14.12, printed pp.282--283.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-solvable-subgroup-flag-realization] to the trivial subgroup of $G$ to obtain a nonzero finite-dimensional $V$ and a faithful closed immersion $r:G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V)$. The trivial subgroup is smooth, connected and solvable, so this application needs no solvability of $G$. The same node gives the projective finite-type complete flag scheme $X=\operatorname{Fl}(V)$. The representation acts by $g(V_i)_i=(r(g)V_i)_i$ on flags. Among the $G(k)$-orbits choose one of least dimension. The boundary assertion of [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry] makes this orbit $O$ closed: a nonempty boundary would contain an orbit of strictly smaller dimension. With its reduced structure $O$ is proper by the closed-subscheme clause of the flag-realization node. Fix $x\in O(k)$ and let $J=G_x$. By [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry], $O\simeq G/J$ as schemes, including a possibly nonsmooth stabilizer $J$.

source.place: Proposition 16.60 proof, first two sentences, printed p.346; Theorem 4.9, p.87; Proposition 1.66, pp.27--28; Propositions 7.29--7.30, pp.146--147.

proof.text: Put $K=(J^0)_{\mathrm{red}}$. The last clause of [lem-sfb-solvable-subgroup-flag-realization] makes $K$ smooth, connected and solvable. By [lem-sfb-nested-homogeneous-quotient-geometry], the map $\pi:Q=G/K\to G/J\simeq O$ is finite and faithfully flat; the source of this map is $G/K$. Finite morphisms are proper by [lem-sfb-affine-proper-finite]. Since $O$ is proper, [lem-weil-pbc-proper-composition] makes $Q$ proper over $k$. This uses neither smoothness of $J$ nor equality of $J$ and $K$.

source.place: Proposition 16.60 proof, third sentence, printed p.346; Proposition 7.15 Cartesian square and Remark 7.16(b), pp.142--143; Appendix A.76(a),(c), pp.583--584. The reversed arrow in the second sentence of Proposition 7.15 is a typographical error, already corrected in the cited nested-quotient node.

proof.text: Since $k$ is algebraically closed it is perfect. By [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus], $K$ has a smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup $K_u$ and torus quotient $D=K/K_u$. Solvability defined by termination of the commutator series supplies the normal series with commutative quotients required there. Viewed as its own ambient group, the solvable group $K$ is a Borel subgroup of $K$. Thus [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy] supplies a maximal torus $T\subseteq K$. Its composite inclusion into $G$ is a torus subgroup, so the hypothesis gives $T=1$. Apply [lem-sfb-solvable-torus-complements] to $K_u\subseteq K$: the restriction $T\to D$ is an isomorphism, hence $D=1$. By the scheme-theoretic kernel clause of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], the kernel of $K\to D$ is $K_u$. As $D=1$, this kernel is all of $K$, proving $K=K_u$ and therefore unipotence of $K$.

source.place: Proposition 16.60 proof, fourth through sixth sentences, p.346; Theorem 16.33(a)--(d), pp.335--336.

proof.text: The explicit faithful geometric-unipotence condition on the smooth group $K$ gives, by [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-unitriangular-embedding], a closed unitriangular embedding; faithfulness here is injectivity on all algebra points. Thus the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-unipotent-homogeneous-quasiaffine] hold for $K\subseteq G$. It gives an immersion $j:Q=G/K\hookrightarrow\mathbf A^n_k$. In particular $j$ is a monomorphism: both a closed immersion and an open immersion are injective on all test-scheme morphisms.

source.place: Proposition 16.60 proof, penultimate sentence, p.346; Proposition 14.26, p.286; Theorem 14.5 and Corollary 14.12, pp.281--283.

proof.text: The scheme $Q$ is separated and of finite type and the quotient map $q:G\to Q$ is faithfully flat by [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry]; it is also of finite presentation by [lem-sfb-nested-homogeneous-quotient-geometry] applied to $1\subseteq K$. Apply [lem-sbc-smooth-flat-surjective-source-descent] to $G\to Q\to\operatorname{Spec}k$: its composite is smooth, so $Q$ is smooth. By [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced], $Q$ is reduced. It is nonempty because of $q(e)$, and connected because $q$ is surjective and $G$ is connected: any disconnection of $Q$ would pull back to two nonempty clopen subsets of $G$.

source.place: Proposition 16.60 proof, last two sentences, p.346; Proposition 7.12, p.141; quotient smoothness and connectedness are made explicit here.

proof.text: The affine space target is separated over $k$, so properness of $Q$ and [lem-weil-pbc-proper-to-separated] make $j$ proper. It is a monomorphism by step 4, hence a closed immersion by [lem-pc-proper-monomorphism-closed]. A closed immersion into an affine scheme is affine by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-integral-separated-uc], so $Q$ is affine. Its proper structure morphism is therefore finite by [lem-sfb-affine-proper-finite].

source.place: Proposition 16.60 proof, final sentence, p.346; Appendix A.75(g), p.583, expanded using Stacks Tag 04XV (etale.tex, lemma-characterize-closed-immersion), Tag 01WN (morphisms.tex, lemma-finite-proper).

proof.text: Write $Q=\operatorname{Spec}B$. By the definition of a finite morphism [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism], $B$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra. Reducedness and nonemptiness of $Q$ say respectively that $B$ has no nonzero nilpotents and $1\ne0$. By connectedness and [lem-pc-scheme-connected-iff-idempotents], its only idempotents are $0,1$. Hence [lem-pc-alg-closed-reduced-algebra-no-idempotents-dim-one] says that $k\to B$ is an isomorphism. Therefore $Q\simeq\operatorname{Spec}k$ as a scheme, not just as a topological space.

source.place: Proposition 16.60 proof, final sentence, p.346; Appendix A.75(g), p.583. The finite reduced connected algebra calculation spells out why this is the rational reduced point.

proof.text: The quotient torsor identity in [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry] identifies the fibre of $q:G\to Q$ over $q(e)$ with $K$: in $G\times K\simeq G\times_QG$, pull back the first factor along the identity point. Since $Q=\operatorname{Spec}k$, that fibre is all of $G$. Thus $K\hookrightarrow G$ is an isomorphism of group schemes. From $K=K_u$ in step 3, $G$ satisfies the faithful geometric-unipotence hypothesis of [lem-sfb-geometric-unipotence-unitriangular-embedding]. Choose its closed immersion $i:G\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_{m,k}$ factoring through $\mathcal U_m$, with $m\geq1$. For $g\in G(k)$ put $A=i(g)-I_m$. This is strictly upper triangular. Every summand of $(A^m)_{ab}$ contains a product indexed by $a<i_1<\cdots<i_{m-1}<b$, impossible among $m$ indices. Hence $A^m=0$. Taking $\rho=i$ and $N=m$ proves precisely the claimed closed faithful representation and nilpotence condition.

The item's 8 steps follow 16.60 sentence by sentence and spell out what it leaves implicit. Step 1: a closed flag orbit of minimal dimension, identified with G/J. Step 2: K=(J^0)_red; G/K->G/J is finite in the correct direction, and the misprinted arrow in 7.15 is noted; this gives Q proper. Step 3: perfect-solvable gives K_u; borel-torus applied to K as its own Borel gives T=1; torus-complements gives D=1; the kernel clause gives K=K_u. Step 4: the unitriangular embedding plus the new node give an immersion j. Step 5: Q is smooth, reduced and connected. Step 6: j is proper and monic, hence a closed immersion; Q is affine, hence finite over k. Step 7: B finite-dimensional, reduced, with no nontrivial idempotents, so B=k. Step 8: the torsor fibre at e gives K=G, and (A)^m=0. I read every cited statement and checked its hypotheses. New node lem-sfb-unipotent-homogeneous-quasiaffine: a true special case of 14.26 (smooth U; the k-point condition is unipotence by 14.12), statement only and self-contained. Tested on U=1, U=G, the unitriangular subgroup of SL2 (quotient A^2 minus 0), and mu_p (excluded by smoothness).
